I've farmed this land for 30 years and I know what works here in Quzhou. The soil is good, the well gives me reliable water, and my main system is the cabbage-eggplant rotation — that stays the same this year. Two mu goes to that rotation. My wife and I can manage 4.5 mu without hired help if I plan the planting calendar carefully so the labor peaks don't stack up.

For eggplant, I transplant in late April after the last frost risk passes. It's my biggest cash earner on that 2 mu plot, so I put more fertilizer and water into it. After I clear the eggplant in August, I plant cabbage on the same 2 mu — the roots break up differently and the pest pressure stays lower than if I grew the same thing twice.

Cauliflower goes in spring on about 0.8 mu. I use hybrids — the heads are more uniform and buyers in the county market pay better for them. Same reasoning for cabbage and eggplant: hybrids. For chili I use improved seed, and for kidney bean and spinach I still use traditional varieties because they've done well for me and the seed cost is low.

Spinach is my winter filler crop — half a mu, not much work, gives us something to sell in the slow months. Kidney bean I grow in spring on half a mu, partly for household use and partly for local sale.

I irrigate from the well. Eggplant is thirsty — I water it 9 times through the season. Cabbage gets 6 irrigations. Spinach is only 4 because winter temperatures reduce evaporation. I spray pesticides when I see pressure building, not on a fixed calendar, but from long experience I know roughly how many rounds each crop ends up needing — eggplant and chili get hit hardest by insects and disease.

I use rotary tillage before each planting. It's what my small hand tractor does best on this soil.
